值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析「臺灣光復」與「軍事佔領」的歷史定位爭端，擺脫非黑即白的政治口號。
  • 循序梳理從《馬關條約》、《開羅宣言》到《波茨坦公告》等關鍵國際條約與文件的法律鏈結。
  • 釐清戰後麥克阿瑟《一般第一號命令》與受降儀式的真實意涵，幫助讀者建立客觀理解臺灣戰後地位的歷史視野。

摘要

歷史爭議的開端與《馬關條約》的割讓

作者指出，每逢10月25日「臺灣光復節」，社會各界常對臺灣究竟是「光復」、「接管」還是「軍事佔領」展開激烈爭論。為了釐清真相，作者認為必須回到1895年的《馬關條約》。清朝在甲午戰爭失敗後，透過正式的國際條約將臺灣與澎湖割讓給日本，這是一項永久性的領土轉移，而非暫時佔領或租借。在此後的50年間，日本在臺推行現代化建設與殖民同化，臺灣人民亦透過武裝抗暴與議會請願等文化運動爭取權利，這段複雜的殖民歷史，成為日後探討臺灣如何「回歸」的歷史原點。

二戰盟軍架構與主權歸屬的法律鏈結

戰局逆轉後的1943年，中華民國、美國與英國共同發表《開羅宣言》，明確宣示日本所竊取之東北、臺灣與澎湖應歸還給中華民國。作者強調，該文件具體寫明的是中華民國而非模糊的中國概念。隨後於1945年發布的《波茨坦公告》第8條進一步確認《開羅宣言》之條件必將實施。隨著日本天皇宣布投降並簽署無條件投降書，在法律與外交脈絡上，中華民國政府據此建立了要求日本履行戰後安排、歸還臺灣澎湖主權的論述依據。

《一般第一號命令》與臺北公會堂受降

二戰結束後，盟軍最高統帥麥克阿瑟發布《一般第一號命令》，依據作戰區域劃分受降代表，明令在中國大陸與臺灣的日軍向蔣介石投降。作者指出，雖然有人主張當時國民政府僅是代表同盟國前來執行軍事受降，但此項軍事接收安排並非孤立產生，而是根植於《開羅宣言》與《波茨坦公告》的戰後框架中。最終在1945年10月25日，臺灣省行政長官陳儀於臺北公會堂（今中山堂）正式接受日軍投降，揭開了戰後臺灣主權轉移與歷史定位爭辯的序幕。

================================================

Whether Taiwan in 1945 was restored or occupied, I don't think we should pretend history is beyond debate. The Cairo Declaration, the Potsdam Proclamation, the San Francisco Peace Treaty, and of course the Treaty of Taipei are all open to discussion. To what extent international law was fulfilled in 1945 is a topic for scholars to present various arguments; a truly free country should never fear its people discussing their own history . But we also don't need to deny that anything happened in 1945 just because of today's political stance. Many often. ask about the map in my background; this isn't just the map of the Republic of China as I dream of it, but the way 1.4 billion descendants of China imagine the Republic should look. We aim to restore the Republic, fulfilling its mission through the Three Principles of the People. We've launched a merchandise set including the map poster, wall scroll, pillow, and ROC flag pin. Why choose when you can have it all? Get them together for just 1911. Orders over 699 on both platforms ship for free. Overseas friends, don't worry—international shipping options are coming soon. Get. yours now! >> Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu. On October 25, 1945, was Taiwan truly restored? Every year on October 25, we hear a familiar name: Taiwan Restoration Day. Although few people call it that nowadays, it’s recently made a comeback. For many, this is how it was taught in history textbooks from childhood. After losing the First Sino-Japanese War in 1895, Taiwan was ceded to Japan. Following 50 years of Japanese rule, the victory in the War of Resistance in 1945 saw Taiwan finally restored and returned to the. Republic of China. Sounds very simple, right? Yet in recent years, whenever Taiwan Restoration is mentioned, someone immediately jumps up to say there was no restoration at all. They claim that in 1945, the Nationalist government was merely representing the Allies to receive Taiwan. Some even argue that Taiwan’s true sovereignty shift didn't happen until the 1951 San Francisco Peace Treaty, which they claim didn't explicitly hand Taiwan to the ROC—thus calling restoration a political myth created by the KMT. So,. who is actually right? What exactly happened at the Taipei Zhongshan Hall on October 25, 1945? Was that the day Japan officially ceded Taiwan to the Republic of China? Or was it simply a ceremony for the Japanese military to surrender? Occupation, reception, restoration, and transfer of sovereignty—are these four terms referring to the same thing? Let’s set aside sides and slogans for today and simply lay out the documents from 1895 to 1952 one by one to examine them . After watching, you may find that " Taiwan Retrocession" is a myth with no historical basis, but interpreting October 25, 1945, as an undisputed transfer of sovereignty under international law is also an oversimplification. True history is more complex than the political slogans of either side. First, we must start from 1895, because if we don't know how Taiwan left China in the first place, we cannot discuss whether its 1945 status was truly a return. The First. Sino-Japanese War broke out in 1894, and the Qing Dynasty suffered a crushing defeat; the following year, they signed the Treaty of Shimonoseki, ceding Taiwan, Penghu, and related islands to Japan. Note that this was not a temporary military occupation or a 99-year lease, but a territorial cession through a formal international treaty signed at the time. Thus, beginning in 1895, Taiwan entered the colonial governing system of the.

Japanese Empire. For the next 50 years, Taiwan underwent political and social developments entirely different from mainland China. The Japanese government established the Governor-General’s Office in Taiwan, built railways, ports , schools, and public health systems, while simultaneously enforcing strict colonial rule, political suppression, and Japanization policies. Taiwanese people resisted Japanese rule through armed conflict, and also sought political rights through petition movements for the establishment of a parliament and cultural movements. Therefore, the 50 years of Japanese. colonial rule cannot be summarized by saying simply that "the infrastructure was good" or "the colonization was cruel"—it is a very complex colonial history. However, one thing is indisputable: the 1895 Treaty of Shimonoseki was indeed the starting point for Taiwan leaving Qing rule. This raises a question: since Taiwan was ceded through an international treaty back then, by what means did it "return" in 1945? The time comes to 1943; by then, the War of Resistance. against Japan had been going on for a long time, and the situation of World War II had gradually begun to reverse. Chairman Chiang Kai-shek of the Republic of China, U.S. President Roosevelt, and British Prime Minister Churchill held a conference in Cairo, Egypt, to discuss the war against Japan and the post-war order in Asia. After the conference, the Cairo Declaration was released, containing a sentence directly relevant to our topic today: it declared that territories Japan had taken from China, such as Manchuria,. Taiwan (Formosa), and the Pescadores ( Penghu Islands), should be restored to the Republic of China. And what is referred to here is the "Republic of China," not some vague "China," and certainly not the People's Republic of China, because the CCP had not even been established in 1943. This text can also be seen directly in the original diplomatic documents preserved by the U.S. Department of State, so from the perspective of the Republic of China government, the Cairo Declaration is extremely important. This signifies that the three main Allied powers—the United States, the United Kingdom, and. the Republic of China—had already declared their political intent regarding the postwar status of Taiwan before the war ended: Taiwan and the Penghu Islands were to be returned to the Republic of China. But the controversy begins here, as some ask whether the Cairo Declaration itself is a formal treaty of territorial transfer or merely a political manifesto by the Allies regarding the postwar order. If it is only a declaration, is it sufficient on its own to cause the transfer of territorial sovereignty? Let us set this question aside for now,. because two years later, a second, more important document appeared. In July 1945, Germany had already surrendered, and Japan became the last remaining major Axis power still at war. The United States, the United Kingdom, and the Republic of China jointly issued the Potsdam Proclamation, demanding Japan's unconditional surrender. Article 8 explicitly stated that the terms of the Cairo Declaration must be carried out and specified that Japan's sovereignty would be limited to Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, Shikoku, and other minor islands as determined by the. Allies. This becomes very important because the Republic of China's argument forms a very clear chain here: the 1943 Cairo Declaration said Taiwan and Penghu should be restored to the Republic of China, and the 1945 Potsdam Proclamation reaffirmed that the terms of the Cairo Declaration must be implemented. Subsequently, Japan accepted the Potsdam Proclamation. On August 15, the Emperor of Japan announced the acceptance of the surrender terms via radio broadcast, and on September 2, Japanese representatives formally signed the Instrument of Surrender aboard the USS.

Missouri in Tokyo Bay. Therefore, from the legal perspective of the Republic of China government, since Japan accepted the Potsdam Proclamation, and the Proclamation required the execution of the Cairo Declaration, the return of Taiwan and Penghu to the Republic of China was a postwar arrangement that Japan was obligated to fulfill after its defeat. This is the most important international documentary basis for today's discourse on Taiwan's retrocession. But then another question arises: after Japan's surrender, to whom were the more than 200,000 Japanese troops in Taiwan supposed to. surrender? After Japan announced its surrender, the Allies faced a very practical problem: the Imperial Japanese Army was spread across Asia, and they couldn't exactly all be told to take ships to Tokyo and line up to surrender, could they? Thus, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers MacArthur issued the famous General Order No. 1, which stipulated that Japanese forces in different regions should surrender to different Allied representatives. For example, Japanese troops in parts of Manchuria and North Korea surrendered to Soviet forces, those in parts of Southeast Asia. surrendered to the British forces, while those in most of mainland China and, most importantly for us today, Taiwan, were explicitly ordered to surrender to Chiang Kai-shek. So, when some say the Nationalist government only came to Taiwan in 1945 to accept the surrender under Allied orders, that statement is partially correct, because the surrender in 1945 did indeed take place under the overall postwar surrender framework of the Allies. But if we take it a step further and claim the Republic of China has absolutely no. connection to Taiwan, and that the U.S. just casually asked Chiang Kai-shek to take over, that is an exaggeration. The Allied decision to have Japanese forces in Taiwan surrender to Chiang Kai-shek was rooted in the postwar framework already established by the Cairo Declaration and the Potsdam Proclamation. In other words, General Order No. 1 directly addressed to whom the Japanese military would surrender. As for how the ultimate sovereignty of Taiwan would be handled, it must be. viewed within the context of the entire body of postwar documents and subsequent treaties; this distinction is crucial. Coming to the date we are actually discussing: October 25, 1945, at 10:00 AM, at the Taipei Public Hall, which is today's Zhongshan Hall in Taipei. The person representing the Republic of China to accept the surrender was Chen Yi, the Chief Executive of Taiwan Province, while the Japanese side was represented by the Governor-General of Taiwan and Commander of the Tenth Area Army, Rikichi Ando. The surrender ceremony was held right there, where Rikichi. Ando formally signed the relevant surrender documents, accepting the orders from the Republic of China. Following this, various Japanese government agencies, military facilities, and administrative systems were handed over, and the Taiwan Provincial Administrative Executive Office of the Republic of China began its operations. Historical materials preserved by the Taiwan Historica also record this surrender ceremony and the subsequent government transition. Moreover, a "Taiwan Retrocession Day" celebration was held that afternoon, which local Taiwanese leader Lin Hsien-tang also attended. In other. words, the term "Retrocession" was not something suddenly invented decades later. At the moment of the change in power in 1945, the Republic of China government and some Taiwanese social leaders already used the term " Retrocession" to understand this political change. In their view, Taiwan , which had been ceded to Japan in 1895 due to defeat in war, had finally ended its Japanese colonial rule and returned to the governance of the Republic of China after China's eight-year war of resistance and the Allies 'war against Japan. Therefore, if someone claims.

that the concept of "Taiwan Retrocession" never existed historically and was just a brainwashing invention by the KMT later on, that does not align with the historical records of the time. However , the question on the other side remains: does the acceptance of the surrender on October 25, 1945, equate to the undisputed transfer of territorial sovereignty under international law on that very day? This is where things truly get complicated; it is a question we cannot avoid. Because in the aftermath of a war, the question of to whom an army. surrenders and the question of who owns a piece of land under international law can fundamentally be two different issues. General Order No. 1 only dictated where to evacuate during a fire, but it didn't mean the security guard giving directions suddenly became the owner of the building. This is why those who argue that Taiwan's status is undetermined, or who question whether a legal transfer was completed in 1945, present a very compelling argument. Accepting the surrender of Japanese forces in Taiwan proves that the Republic of China achieved the status of actual occupation and administration , but the surrender order itself is not a peace treaty that cedes territory. This challenge cannot be dismissed simply by labeling someone a "Taiwan independence supporter," because to truly discuss international law, one must examine the peace treaty formally signed by Japan after the war: the 1951 San Francisco Peace Treaty. On September 8, 1951, Japan and several Allied nations signed the peace treaty. in San Francisco, USA. Article 2 of this treaty clearly states that Japan renounces all rights, titles, and claims to Taiwan and the Penghu Islands . This sentence is actually very important; it formally confirms that Japan no longer possesses sovereignty over Taiwan and Penghu. It is like a landlord signing a contract to move out , but leaving the section for the new tenant blank. The treaty does not state that Japan ceded Taiwan and Penghu to the Republic of China, nor does it state they were ceded to the People's. Republic of China; it only states that Japan renounces them. This is the reason why the international legal dispute over Taiwan's postwar status has persisted. Those who argue that Taiwan's status is undetermined would say, "Look, if the Allied nations believed sovereignty was transferred to the Republic of China in 1945, why didn't the formal 1951 peace treaty simply state clearly that Taiwan belongs to the Republic of China?" Supporters of the Republic of China's restoration would counter that the direction of Taiwan's return was already determined by the Cairo. Declaration, the Potsdam Proclamation, and the Japanese surrender, and the Republic of China had effectively ruled Taiwan since 1945. The function of the San Francisco Treaty was for Japan to formally renounce its rights once again when peace was officially restored between Japan and the Allied nations. The two sides developed different interpretations from this point on, and the international political context of that era cannot be ignored. The China of 1951 was completely different from the China of 1945. The Chinese Communist Party took control of mainland China in 1949, and the. Republic of China government moved to Taiwan. At that time, should Taipei or Beijing have been invited to represent China at the San Francisco conference? This became a huge political issue under the Cold War. Ultimately, neither side signed the San Francisco Treaty. Therefore, the fact that the treaty did not designate a recipient for Taiwan was not just a purely legal technicality; it had a very profound Cold War political background. Therefore, if anyone tells you that there is absolutely nothing to discuss.

regarding the Taiwan sovereignty issue in international law, regardless of which side they support, I believe they are oversimplifying history. The Republic of China's narrative certainly does not stop at the San Francisco Peace Treaty. On April 28, 1952, the Republic of China and Japan signed the Treaty of Peace between the Republic of China and Japan in Taipei, commonly known as the "Sino-Japanese Peace Treaty" or the "Treaty of Taipei." Article 1 of this treaty formally ended the state of war between the Republic of China and Japan, while Article 2. confirmed that, in accordance with the San Francisco Peace Treaty, Japan had renounced all rights, titles, and claims to Taiwan and the Penghu Islands . Even more interesting is Article 10, which stipulates that for the purposes of this treaty, inhabitants of Taiwan and the Penghu Islands—including their descendants—shall be deemed Republic of China nationals, provided they possess Republic of China nationality under the laws currently in force in those territories. Other parts of the treaty also directly use terms such as "the authorities of the Republic of China in Taiwan and the. Penghu Islands." Therefore, the Republic of China government has long maintained that the Sino-Japanese Peace Treaty, when linked with the preceding Cairo Declaration, the Japanese Instrument of Surrender, and the 1945 takeover, further affirms the Republic of China's status over Taiwan and Penghu. However, skeptics still point out that Article 2 of the Sino-Japanese Peace Treaty does not use the specific phrasing "Japan cedes Taiwan to the Republic of China," but rather reaffirms that Japan has already renounced it. Thus, while this treaty serves as vital evidence for the. Republic of China's legal arguments, it did not eliminate all differing interpretations of international law. This is exactly where I believe we need to be most honest when discussing this history today. At this point, we can finally answer the question that has circulated online for years: Was the event in Taiwan in 1945 a "takeover" or "retrocession"? I believe this question itself sets up a false dichotomy. This is because "surrender" describes a military act, where the Japanese military surrendered to Republic of. China representatives; "takeover" describes an administrative act, where the ROC government assumed control of existing administrative institutions, property, and military facilities in Taiwan to establish its own governance; and "retrocession" describes the political and historical significance that the Republic of China and segments of Taiwanese society at the time attributed to this historical change. These three terms can actually coexist. On October 25, 1945, the surrender did indeed occur, the takeover did indeed begin, and the Republic of China government, along with those who. support this national identity, did indeed refer to this event as Taiwan's retrocession. The true point of contention is a fourth level: Can October 25, 1945, also be defined as the day when all sovereign processes under international law were completed without dispute? On this point, we must acknowledge that there are different legal interpretations. I believe a more precise understanding is that Taiwan's retrocession is a political and historical concept of the Republic of China with a very clear background and. historical basis. However, if it is interpreted as the indisputable completion of all sovereign transfer procedures under international law on October 25, 1945, then one must face the controversies left behind by post-war peace treaties. This may not be as satisfying as a political slogan, but history itself is not meant for our gratification. Another thing I think must be made clear is that acknowledging 1945 as the end of Japanese colonial rule—which holds the historical significance of retrocession—does not mean we must.

glorify the governance of the Republic of China government after it took over Taiwan; these two matters can be completely separated. Many Taiwanese in 1945 did indeed have expectations for the end of the war and the new regime, but these expectations soon collided with a very cruel reality. The Taiwanese people at the time eagerly welcomed the central government, only to be met with skyrocketing prices, official corruption, chaotic administrative takeovers, and cultural and political estrangement between mainland officials and local society,. eventually sparking the 228 Incident tragedy within just two years. Today, when state archives compile materials on the 228 Incident, they also explicitly list administrative corruption, inflation, discriminatory treatment, poor governance, and social alienation as important background factors of the event. Therefore, we do not need to defend the mistakes of the early government just because we identify with the Republic of China, and we certainly do not need to erase the pain of the victims. I have always believed that those who truly have confidence in a country do not need to rely on concealing the mistakes the. country has made to uphold its dignity. The history of the Republic of China has aspects worth being proud of, but it also has parts that must be reflected upon; both can exist simultaneously. Ultimately, I think what is truly worth asking is not whether we can talk about Taiwan's retrocession, because calling it retrocession, a post-war takeover, or a transfer of power reflects different historical perspectives and national identities. What is truly worth understanding is that 1945 was indeed. an undeniable, massive rupture in Taiwanese history. The Japanese Empire's 50-year colonial rule ended, the Republic of China government began its actual governance of Taiwan, and Taiwan re-entered the political and constitutional history of the Republic of China. But the most interesting part of history is that the central government that arrived in Taiwan in 1945 had not yet fulfilled the republican ideals it claimed to uphold. The Republic of China at the time was still in the midst of war, followed by the outbreak of the Chinese Civil War, and the central government experienced. long periods of martial law and authoritarian rule after relocating to Taiwan. If the story stops here, then retrocession was merely the departure of one ruler. Yet, the true value of the Republic of China for us today lies in the fact that its story did not end in 1945. The Republic of China adopted a constitution in 1946 and implemented it in 1947. Although constitutional rule was severely distorted by the civil war and martial law, the nation returned to democratization after the 1980s, lifting martial law, allowing. new parties, holding full parliamentary elections, electing the president directly, achieving peaceful transfers of power, and ensuring freedom of speech and local autonomy. Today, we can even openly criticize the president every day, support unification or independence, back a political party, or support none at all; this is what I believe is most worth reflecting on when examining history. When Dr. Sun Yat-sen launched the revolution, his true goal was never just to drive out the Qing government. If a revolution. only replaces one emperor with another who cannot be removed by the people, then the revolution has not been completed at all. Therefore, within the Three Principles of the People, beyond nationalism, there is the vital Principle of Democracy. A nation’s purpose is not merely territorial integrity, but rather to make the people the masters of the country. So, if I were to reinterpret the term " retrocession"(Guangfu) today, I would say it actually has two layers. The first layer is the retrocession of territory. Taiwan was ceded in 1895 due.

to defeat, and in 1945, after Japan’s defeat, the ROC government arrived to accept the surrender, ending 50 years of colonial rule. This is the most direct historical source for why we commemorate October 25th today. However , there is a second and, in my view, more difficult retrocession: the retrocession of civil rights. Changing a flag over a piece of land does not mean the people immediately gain freedom. Post-1945 Taiwan still endured the 228 Incident, the White Terror, long-term martial law, and an era where. the government could ban parties and restrict speech, with people unable to directly choose their national leader. Therefore, if we look at the entire history of the Republic of China in Taiwan over a longer period, I believe 1945 only completed the first phase. The Free Area truly moved toward becoming a free China step by step through the democratization process of the following decades. Thus, in commemorating Taiwan's retrocession today, I do not think we should pretend that history is devoid of controversy. The Cairo Declaration can be discussed, the Potsdam Proclamation can be. discussed, the San Francisco Peace Treaty can be discussed, and the Treaty of Taipei can certainly be discussed as well. The extent to which 1945 fulfilled international legal requirements is a subject that allows for different scholars to offer different arguments. A truly free nation should never fear its people discussing their own history. But we also have no need, based on today’s political stances, to go to the other extreme and pretend that nothing happened in 1945. What we should really be doing is not using today's political stance to cherry-pick a version of 1945. that we like, but to view the entire history as a whole. Because the Republic of China has traveled for over a hundred years, through revolution, war, civil strife, and authoritarianism , finally proving one thing in the free areas of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen, and Matsu: a Chinese society can be democratic, a Chinese nation can practice constitutionalism, and the people can use their ballots to choose a government and peaceably replace it. This is also why I have always believed that guarding the Republic of China today should not just be about holding onto a title, a flag, or a specific. historical memory; what we must truly safeguard is a free China. It is a China where the state belongs to the people, not the people to a party; a China where the government is bound by a constitution, the military serves the nation, and the people are free to speak, protest, and choose their own future. And if one day the over one billion people on the mainland can also freely choose their government and criticize their leaders without fear, then to me, that would perhaps be a more complete fulfillment of civil. rights after over 100 years of the National Revolution. Our Founding Father launched the revolution not just to reclaim territory, but to establish a republic that is truly of the people, by the people, and for the people. This path has been interrupted countless times—defeated by warlords, by foreign aggression, by civil war, and even by ourselves. But at least today in Taiwan, we have proven that this path is not impossible. As long as there are still people who believe in democratic constitutionalism and the republic, and as long as the embers of. a free China have not been extinguished , this political journey that began with the Xinhai Revolution has not yet reached its end.
